pos.personaBrief: Meisl was an 'ardent defender of the passing game, ball on the ground' (Trivela) and Austria's 'famous combination play' and 'Kombinationsgabe' (WSC, 1932 Times) point to a side built on keeping and circulating the ball rather than waiting to counter.

pro.personaBrief: Short, flat passes taken from the Scots (de.wikipedia), an attacking centre-half who fed the forwards (WSC, Trivela) and an 'unwillingness to dribble' or go individual when passing broke down describe patient ground combination, not direct or aerial play.

est.personaBrief: The 'interchanging of the five forward players' (These Football Times), 'the player with the ball is supported by his team-mates' (Game of the People) and a deep-lying centre-forward in Sindelar point to a relational, close-combination attack inside a nominal 2-3-5.

lar.personaBrief: No verified width evidence; from general knowledge the 2-3-5 kept two wingers, but the Danubian game ran through combinations around Sindelar and the inside forwards and dispensed with aerial passing, so crosses were not the main route; consistent with the verified ground-passing facts.

blo.personaBrief: The only defensive fact is England being 'baffled by Austria's retreating defence' (WSC, 1932), with no pressing evidence; the team dropped back and regrouped rather than pressing high.

mar.personaBrief: No source describes Austria's marking; the contrast 'Pozzo's man-marking, bruising, steamroller versus Meisl's Danubian waltz' (Irish Times) suggests Austria were not man-markers, so answers lean to space-based defending of the 2-3-5 era.

pla.personaBrief: 'Spüts euer Spüü!' at 0-2 down at Stamford Bridge and 'Austria concentrated on their waltz' while Pozzo planned a blitz (Untold Game, 1934) show a coach who kept his own game regardless of opponent, despite talk of studying many systems.

res.personaBrief: Meisl championed passing football that was 'intelligent, fluid and aesthetically pleasing' (Trivela) and the Wunderteam is remembered for its style more than trophies; Pozzo is the pragmatic contrast.

sis.personaBrief: The disciplinarian Meisl long left out Sindelar (SI, Goldblatt) and his side was collective combination with 'no individual effort' and an 'unwillingness to dribble' (WSC), so the system outweighed individual licence, though it relied on technical players.

jog.personaBrief: Sindelar 'no brawn but any amount of brain' (Willy Meisl) and the passing centre-half Smistik show a technical team, even if Meisl earlier preferred a strong English-type centre-forward like Uridil (These Football Times).

bas.personaBrief: Meisl 'hesitated to go on breaking the mould' with Sindelar (Irish Times) and took a 1934 squad where 'most were the wrong side of 30' (Untold Game), bringing in a 31-year-old Horvath: he trusted experienced, homegrown Austrian players.

lid.personaBrief: Described as a 'staunch disciplinarian' who 'cast adrift' Sindelar and was 'tobend' at his answer (SI, de.wikipedia); he gave in to journalists in 1931 grumbling, not to players.
